h2: Pipeline integrity inspection: ILI verification digs and field NDE
html:
Pipeline integrity inspection, as US and Canadian operators buy it, is mostly field NDE at an excavation. The in-line inspection (ILI) tool has reported an anomaly, the operator has put it on a dig list, and someone has to measure what is really there. Atlantis NDT does that measurement work. We do not run in-line inspection tools; the operator's ILI vendor does, and our measurements are what the operator uses to check the tool's calls.

What happens at an ILI verification dig

Once the pipe is exposed and the coating removed, the in-ditch examination usually follows the same sequence. The feature is located from the girth-weld count and the ILI reference marks, then measured: UT thickness on a grid across the corroded area, corrosion mapping with encoded UT or phased array where the area is large or irregular, pit-depth gauging for external corrosion, and wet fluorescent magnetic particle inspection to look for stress corrosion cracking colonies and for cracks at dents and seam welds. Where crack depth matters, it is sized with PAUT or TOFD. Each measurement is tied to the ILI feature number so the operator can compare tool and field values feature by feature.

Why ILI verification data matters to the operator

API 1163 asks operators to confirm that an ILI system performed to its stated specification, and the usual evidence is field data from verification digs plotted against the tool's predictions. Under 49 CFR 192 Subpart O and 49 CFR 195.452 in the US, and CSA Z662 in Canada, the operator's integrity engineer then assesses each feature, typically with ASME B31G or RSTRENG for corrosion. That assessment, and any repair decision, stays with the operator's engineer. Our part is a measurement record that stands up in an audit: procedure, calibration, technician certification, a sketch with clock position and distance from the reference weld, and the raw grid readings.

Touch point corrosion at pipe supports

Above ground, the corrosion that most often escapes routine thickness surveys is touch point corrosion, where pipe rests on a support and water is trapped against the bottom of the pipe. It cannot be seen on a walkdown. Programmes find it by lifting the pipe off the support for a direct visual and UT check, or by screening with a long-range technique the owner specifies and then proving up each indication with UT or PAUT at the support. API 570 and API RP 574 both list supports among the locations a piping inspection plan should cover. Damage under insulation is covered on corrosion under insulation.

Scoping a dig programme

Send the dig list with the ILI feature types, the pipe grade and wall, the coating type and your procedure requirements. We will confirm the method for each feature type, the certification your procedure requires (SNT-TC-1A or CP-189 Level II, with Level III review) and how results come back to you. For how magnetic flux leakage tools find metal loss in the first place, see MFL corrosion inspection for pipelines; for the regulatory background, read the guide to ILI dig verification and API 1163. To discuss a programme, contact the inspection team.
